title: Understanding HOA Board Elections and Voting Rights Under the Davis-Stirling Act
content_html:
If you own a home in a planned community in Temecula, Murrieta, or Menifee, chances are your homeowners association is governed by a state law known as the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act. For many homeowners, HOA board elections are the one piece of association governance they interact with directly — a ballot shows up, a meeting gets scheduled, and then a handful of neighbors are suddenly making decisions about assessments, maintenance, and rule enforcement for the whole community. Understanding how those elections are supposed to work can help you participate more meaningfully, whether you're voting, running for a seat, or just trying to make sense of an association you're about to buy into.

What the Davis-Stirling Act Covers

The Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act is the body of California law that governs common interest developments — condominiums, planned developments, and other communities with HOAs. It is codified in the California Civil Code and addresses a wide range of topics: assessments, architectural review, meetings, disclosures, and — relevant here — the rules associations must follow when electing their boards of directors.[1]

Before Davis-Stirling's election provisions were strengthened, HOA elections in California varied enormously from association to association, with inconsistent rules about secret ballots, candidate qualifications, and who could oversee the count. The law was amended specifically to standardize election procedures and reduce disputes over fairness and transparency.

Secret Ballot Elections Are the Default

One of the most significant protections under the Act is the requirement that board elections — along with votes on assessments and other specified matters — generally be conducted by secret ballot.[2] This means an association cannot simply ask for a show of hands at an open meeting or tally verbal votes in front of other members. Instead, the law lays out a structured process: ballots and voting instructions must be mailed or delivered to every member, double-envelope procedures are used to separate a member's identity from their actual vote, and an independent third party or a volunteer committee of members (who are not candidates and not related to candidates) typically handles the count. This structure exists to prevent a board — or anyone with influence over the board — from knowing how individual members voted, which protects members from retaliation and keeps the process credible.

Who Can Vote

Voting rights in an HOA election generally belong to members in good standing as defined by the association's governing documents — typically, the recorded owner of a unit or lot within the community. Each separate interest (each home) usually carries one vote, though the specifics of how voting power is allocated, and how it's handled when a property has multiple owners, are spelled out in the association's Covenants, Conditions & Restrictions (CC&Rs) and bylaws. If you're buying into a community, it's worth reviewing those governing documents during escrow so you understand exactly how voting rights attach to your specific property. Our guide to understanding HOA fees before you buy covers some of the other financial and governance details worth reviewing at the same time.

Candidate Nomination and Qualification Rules

The Act also addresses how associations nominate and qualify candidates for the board. Associations are required to adopt specific election rules covering nomination procedures, candidate qualifications, and the voting process itself, and those rules must be distributed to members before voting begins.[3] An association generally cannot impose candidate qualifications that are arbitrary or disconnected from the legitimate operation of the board — this was an area of significant litigation and legislative attention, since some associations attempted to use eligibility rules to exclude particular candidates or outcomes they disfavored.

If you're considering running for your board, start by requesting a copy of the association's current election rules and any amendments. These documents should explain nomination deadlines, any disclosure requirements for candidates, and how write-in or self-nomination is handled.

Quorum, Proxies, and Ballot Counting

Associations typically need to meet a quorum — a minimum level of member participation — before an election result is valid, though the specific quorum requirement is set by each association's own bylaws rather than a single statewide number. Because turnout can be a challenge in larger communities, many associations rely heavily on mailed ballots rather than requiring members to attend an in-person meeting to vote.

Proxies — where one member authorizes another person to vote on their behalf — are allowed in many contexts but are handled differently from the secret ballot itself, and governing documents typically specify limits on how proxies may be used in board elections specifically. If proxy voting matters to you, check your association's bylaws directly rather than assuming the rules match a different community you've lived in before.

Ballot counting is meant to happen at a noticed open meeting, so that members can observe the process even though they cannot see how any individual voted. Associations are also required to retain ballots and related election materials for a period of time after the election, which matters if a result is ever challenged.

What Happens When Members Dispute an Election

Disputes over HOA elections do happen — over candidate eligibility, ballot handling, notice requirements, or vote counting. The Act provides a legal pathway for members to challenge an election they believe violated these procedural protections, including the ability to bring the dispute to court.[4] Because these disputes can be fact-specific and the remedies available depend on the exact violation alleged, a homeowner who believes an election was mishandled should review the governing documents and the specific statutory provisions carefully, and consult an attorney who handles common interest development law, rather than relying on general assumptions about what the law requires.

Why This Matters When You're Buying or Already Own in an HOA

For buyers, understanding board election mechanics is really part of a broader exercise: understanding how much influence you'll have, as a future owner, over decisions that affect your monthly costs and your property's rules. A community with a transparent, well-run election process is often a reasonable proxy for an association that takes its other governance obligations seriously too. For current owners, participating in board elections — whether by voting, asking questions about the association's election rules, or running for a seat yourself — is one of the more direct ways to influence how your HOA is managed over time.

If you're evaluating a home in a planned community as part of a purchase, it's worth building HOA document review into your overall due diligence alongside other common disclosures. Our overview of seller disclosure requirements in California explains how HOA-related documents typically fit into that broader disclosure picture.
